---
title: "The Decline of Catholic Electoral Distinctiveness in U.S. Presidential Elections, 1948–2024"
description: "Working paper — Catholic presidential vote choice across twenty elections"
date: "2026-05-01"
categories: [Catholic]
---

::: {.justified}

Catholics were once among the most reliably Democratic constituencies in American politics.
Using the American National Election Studies Cumulative File, I track Catholic presidential vote choice across twenty elections from 1948 to 2024.
The Catholic Democratic advantage peaked in 1960, narrowed steadily, and reversed: by 2024 Catholics were slightly less Democratic than the electorate as a whole.
Blinder-Oaxaca decompositions and nested logistic models show that party identification is the primary mediator of this decline, with ideology and issue attitudes absorbing much of what remains.
Affect toward social groups mediates further, and the residual Catholic coefficient turns negative once it is controlled.
The aggregate trend conceals a divided electorate: white Catholics have moved Republican while Hispanic Catholics have not, observant Catholics have moved right while nominal Catholics have not, and generational replacement compounds both.
Catholics remain cross-pressured, culturally conservative and economically progressive in a way that maps cleanly onto neither party.
A multilevel model with partial pooling finds no stable, time-invariant Catholic effect on Democratic voting.
Catholic electoral exceptionalism is a historically bounded phenomenon rather than a permanent feature of American politics.

:::

**Presented.**

- "The Politics of American Catholics" — New Directions in American History, University of Chicago, Spring 2026
